analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Patriot Act and FISA Amendments Act and requires warrants to spy on Americans.
analysis.headline: The Surveillance State Repeal Act, with 15 cosponsors from both parties, was referred to eight House committees and never received a vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the USA PATRIOT Act and the FISA Amendments Act of 2008, the two laws behind much of the government's post-9/11 spying apparatus, and restore the law as it stood before them. Going forward, no information about a U.S. person could be collected under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act or under Executive Order 12333 without a warrant based on probable cause, and data already gathered on Americans that isn't tied to an active investigation would have to be destroyed. It would also bar the government from forcing tech companies to build backdoors into encryption, and would protect intelligence community whistleblowers who report waste, abuse, or lawbreaking.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans: their communications could no longer be collected in bulk or targeted without a warrant, data collected on them without a warrant would be destroyed, their phones and software could not be forced to include government backdoors, and intelligence employees or contractors who report abuses would gain legal protection from retaliation.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the USA PATRIOT Act and the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 and restores the law as those acts found it, undoing the legal basis for post-9/11 surveillance programs.

Prohibits collecting any information relating to a U.S. person under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, or targeting a U.S. person under Executive Order 12333, without a warrant based on probable cause.

Requires the Director of National Intelligence and the Attorney General to destroy information about U.S. persons collected under the repealed laws or without a warrant that is not tied to an investigation actively underway.
Bars the federal government from requiring makers of electronic devices or software to build in a mechanism letting the government bypass encryption or privacy technology.

Lets intelligence community employees and contractors report waste, fraud, abuse, or lawbreaking in FISA programs to the GAO or the intelligence committees, and prohibits retaliation against them, with sanctions up to termination for violators.
Directs the Government Accountability Office to audit and report annually on the government's compliance with surveillance law, including collections under Executive Order 12333.

analysis.who_pays: Intelligence agencies would lose bulk-collection authorities and would have to destroy stockpiles of collected data on Americans; surveillance contractors and the portions of the telecom industry that support those programs would lose business. The counterweight is that the government would lose surveillance tools it has described as counterterrorism assets, and the bill would still allow warrant-based spying on any target, including the power to compel companies to assist and keep the surveillance secret.

drawbacks.text: The repeal is blunt rather than targeted: wiping out the Patriot Act and the FISA Amendments Act wholesale restores the law as it stood before those acts, removing surveillance authorities across the board rather than just the bulk-collection programs critics objected to.

Even as it narrows spying on Americans, the bill keeps and even reinforces the government's power to compel any carrier, landlord, or other person to help conduct secret electronic surveillance of a target, whatever device or service that target uses.

Extending FISA judges' maximum terms from seven to ten years and making them eligible for reappointment could deepen the tenure of the small, closed group of judges who approve government surveillance requests.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the gains are substantial and concrete: a probable-cause warrant before the government collects on an American, deletion of collected data not tied to a real investigation, no forced encryption backdoors, and real whistleblower protection. The cost is that intelligence agencies lose broad tools in ways that go beyond the most controversial programs, and the bill does nothing to loosen the secret, company-compelled surveillance that remains. On balance it is a strong privacy bill, though a blunt one — and it never came anywhere near becoming law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to eight House committees and various subcommittees on the day it was introduced; no committee ever voted it out, and the House never took it up before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Pocan (D-WI) introduced the bill on March 19, 2015, joined by four other original cosponsors: Reps. Massie (R-KY), Grayson (D-FL), McGovern (D-MA), and Doggett (D-TX).

The same day, it was referred to eight House committees — Judiciary, Intelligence, Financial Services, Foreign Affairs, Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Armed Services — a structure that requires multiple committees to act before the full House can consider the bill.

Over the following months it was referred to subcommittees on Crime, Communications and Technology, Highways and Transit, Railroads, and Workforce Protections; the last referral came on November 16, 2015.
The bill attracted 15 cosponsors, 13 Democrats and 2 Republicans, but no committee held a markup or vote, and no floor action ever occurred.
That referral on November 16, 2015 was the last action of any kind; the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The intelligence agencies and surveillance contractors whose programs and data the bill would have eliminated. Because the bill never got a vote, the Patriot Act and FISA authorities it targeted stayed on the books, the collected data it would have required destroyed stayed in government hands, and no encryption-backdoor ban or whistleblower protections took effect.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: The committee of primary referral and its chair
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence leadership
against.role: The committee with jurisdiction over surveillance law and its chair
against.what_they_did: Took no action on a bill that would have repealed the FISA Amendments Act, one of the committee's core jurisdictions.

against.name: House Speaker
against.role: Presiding officer controlling the House floor schedule
against.what_they_did: The bill's eight-committee referral meant no single panel was responsible for moving it, and the House leadership never brought it to the floor in the two years it was pending.

sides.party_line_note: The 15 cosponsors split 13 Democrats and 2 Republicans, so support was bipartisan but tiny in both parties; with no votes ever held, the broader House's position was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill would repeal the laws authorizing much of the government's post-9/11 collection apparatus and force destruction of data on Americans gathered under it, directly threatening programs and the contractor workforce that supports them. Their interest in keeping those programs runs against the public's interest in warrants before surveillance of Americans.

industries.industry: Telecom carriers and communications service providers
industries.note: The bill keeps, and extends across any device or service, the legal duty to help the government conduct secret surveillance of targets on request. But repeal of the bulk-collection framework would end some programs whose legal accommodation these companies administered, reducing both the assistance burden and the legal cover they received under it.

The bill bars the federal government from requiring backdoors into encryption or privacy technology, letting these companies sell secure products without a government-mandated weak point. That weakness would have affected every customer, so the industry's interest here runs with users' interests.
